newsitem.title: USA: Hometown supporters celebrate Clinton's victory.
newsitem.headline: Hometown supporters celebrate Clinton's victory.

text.p: A festive mood gripped President Bill Clinton's hometown on Tuesday night as Clinton and his most loyal supporters followed election returns that made him the first Democrat to win re-election 52 years.

Television networks projected Democrat Clinton the winner over Republican Bob Dole about an hour after most of the polls closed in the eastern United States. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was projected to finish a distant third.

When the race was called, Clinton was in a staff suite on the 18th floor of the Excelsior Hotel, his election headquarters, and walked around the room embracing staff members, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "Obviously, the president is in very good spirits," he told reporters.

Asked if Clinton would meet his vanquished rival in the near future, McCurry said: "You've heard on many occasions the president say how much he respects Senator Dole and admires his service to the nation ... (but) it's premature at this point to talk about how that relationship will develop.
Even before the voting ended, a large exuberant crowd had gathered outside Clinton's hotel, turning downtown Little Rock streets into one big party.
As many as 80,000 people were expected to gather outside the adjacent Old State House -- a large white Greek Revival structure where Clinton planned to claim victory.
For Arkansans, Clinton's duplication of a feat no Democrat managed since Franklin Roosevelt was re-elected in 1944, represented a rehabilitation of sorts.

They had watched in dismay as the image of their state to a beating from the Whitewater case and other scandals that brought disaster to many native sons who accompanied Clinton to Washington after he wrested the White House from then-President George Bush in 1992.

The list of Arkansas casualties during Clinton's first term was long and grim -- deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, a Clinton friend from kindergarten, killed himself; Assistanty Attorney General Webb Hubbell, a onetime law partner of Hillary Rodham Clinton, went to jail; and several other Friends of Bill, including former Surgeon General Joycelyn Elders, were sacked.
But those dark memories were all eclipsed by their former governor's big moment. McCurry said Clinton regarded his triumph at the polls as "a somewhat humbling experience."
"He knows he's going to have to work every day" to meet the challenges facing the country as it prepares to enter the 21st century, the spokesman said.

With the election in hand, attention focused on the people who will surround Clinton for the next four years. White House chief of staff Leon Panetta is among those departing -- he wants to go home to California and perhaps run for governor there in 1996.
Former Small Business Administration chief Erskine Bowles leads the list of possible replacements, but is retreating Clinton's entreaties to return to government service, White House sources said.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, one of many cabinet officers in Little Rock for the victory party, was also expected to step down. Sources said former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright and former assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the Bosnia peace agreement, were on the short list of contenders for Christopher's job.
